title: Written down
hookLine: in the first century BCE the Pali canon was written on palm leaves at Aluvihara

cards: A strip of dried palm leaf, long and narrow, lies across a monk's knee. He scratches letters into it with a metal stylus, line after careful line.

Later, soot and oil are rubbed across the leaf and wiped away, and the dark stays only in the scratches, so the words appear. A whole library can be made this way, one leaf at a time, tied between wooden boards.
In Sri Lanka, the chronicle says, there came a day when the monks decided the teaching had to be written down in books.

teach.h: A TEACHING THAT LIVED IN VOICES.
teach.b: First, a teaching that lived in voices.
Monks learned the discourses and the rules by heart and chanted them together, so one person's mistake could be caught by the others.
The chronicles of Sri Lanka say the three baskets of the teaching, and the commentaries on them, had been handed down that way, by mouth. Second, the fear.
The Mahavamsa sets this moment in the reign of King Vattagamani, a troubled reign in which the king himself is driven from his throne for a time.

The monks saw that people were falling away, the chronicle says, so they came together and wrote the texts down in books, that the true teaching might endure. That's the whole reason it gives. Not convenience.
Tradition names it as Aluvihara, a monastery among great rocks, and pilgrims still visit. Fourth, what changed and what didn't.
Writing didn't end the chanting. Monks still learn texts by heart and recite them together, and in monasteries today the voice is still one way the teaching is received.
But now there was a second, quieter keeper: leaves in a bundle, waiting for anyone who could read. When a manuscript wore out, it could be copied fresh.
That's how a text stays alive, the way a tree does: not by never changing, but by being renewed. The monks at Aluvihara didn't know who would read their leaves.
They wrote for strangers, so the teaching wouldn't depend on any one memory, or any one life.

how: Theravada monasteries keep both ways alive: monks memorize and chant the texts together, and the written canon, once kept on palm leaves, is now printed and studied as well.

practice: With paper and a pen, or a note on your phone, choose one line that matters to you, from these lessons, from someone you love, or from a text of your own tradition.
Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk scratched each letter into the leaf, then read it back once and let it rest with you while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Written down. The moment, as the chronicle tells it, when the teaching carried by voices was set down in books, so it would endure.
